concentration.area: Brussels — detrained 27–28 August after release from Schleswig

sources.note: Chapter 12, the events in Belgium: the corps was still on the railway to Tirlemont on 25 August when Beseler drew its detrained and detraining troops forward through Louvain to Bueken; the rising at Louvain on the 26th delayed the rest of its detrainment; and on 30 August it crossed the Willebroek canal, the 17th Reserve Division by Zellik to Assche and the 18th through Brussels to Ganshoren, leaving one brigade to garrison Brussels. The volume therefore has the corps detraining at Tirlemont and Louvain from 25 August, not at Brussels on 27–28 August.

name: French 1st Army

concentration.area: Épinal–Belfort, the right of the Plan XVII concentration

summary: VII, VIII, XIII, XIV and XXI Corps with the 6th and 8th Cavalry Divisions and the 44th (Alpine) Division. Plan XVII's right: into Alsace towards Sarrebourg, beaten back on 20 August, then held the Vosges and the Trouée de Charmes. The VII Corps went to the Army of Alsace and then the 6th Army.

sources.note: Appendix 3, 'Order of Battle of the French Armies in August 1914': the army's commander, its corps with their divisions, its group of reserve divisions and its cavalry, as of August 1914.

The IX Corps went to the 4th Army and the XVIII to the 5th in the shift north.

sources.note: Appendix 3, 'Order of Battle of the French Armies in August 1914': the army's commander, its corps with their divisions, its group of reserve divisions and its cavalry, as of August 1914.

sources.note: Appendix 3, 'Order of Battle of the French Armies in August 1914': the army's commander, its corps with their divisions, its group of reserve divisions and its cavalry, as of August 1914.

name: French 4th Army

concentration.area: Sainte-Menehould–Bar-le-Duc, the strategic reserve behind the centre

summary: XII and XVII Corps and the Colonial Corps at first, reinforced by the II, XI and IX Corps as the 5th shifted north; 9th Cavalry Division. The Ardennes on 21–23 August (Neufchâteau, Rossignol), the Meuse at Sedan, the Marne around Vitry-le-François.

sources.note: Appendix 3, 'Order of Battle of the French Armies in August 1914': the army's commander, its corps with their divisions, its group of reserve divisions and its cavalry, as of August 1914.

name: French 5th Army

concentration.area: Mézières–Sedan–Rethel, then north to the Sambre–Meuse angle

summary: I, II, III, X and XI Corps, the 4th Group of Reserve Divisions (51st, 53rd, 69th) and Sordet's Cavalry Corps on the left. Moved north to face the German right: Charleroi, Guise, the retreat; under Franchet d'Espèrey from 3 September, the Marne at Montmirail.

sources.note: Appendix 3, 'Order of Battle of the French Armies in August 1914': the army's commander, its corps with their divisions, its group of reserve divisions and its cavalry, as of August 1914.

name: French 6th Army

sources.note: The footnote on the Sixth Army: 'It consisted on the 5th September of the VII. Corps (14th and 63rd Reserve Divisions), 45th Division, 55th and 56th Reserve Divisions, the Moroccan Brigade, and Gillet's cavalry brigade — some 70,000 men, with Sordet's cavalry corps attached. Behind it were a group of Territorial brigades under General Mercier-Milon, Ebener's Group of Reserve divisions (61st and 62nd), and the actual garrison of Paris.' Edmonds's 70,000 for 5 September is well under the 150,000 this card gives.

name: French 9th Army

concentration.area: Formed 5 September from the Foch Detachment between the 4th and 5th Armies, around Sézanne–Fère-Champenoise

summary: IX and XI Corps, the 42nd Division, the Moroccan Division, the 52nd and 60th Reserve Divisions and the 9th Cavalry Division. The marshes of Saint-Gond, 6–9 September, against Bülow's left and Hausen's Saxons.

name: Army of Alsace

concentration.area: Belfort and the Upper Alsace front

summary: Formed 10 August under Pau from the VII Corps, the 44th Division, the 8th Cavalry Division and reserve divisions; retook Mulhouse on 19 August, and was dissolved on 26 August when Joffre sent its corps west to the new 6th Army.

name: Army of Lorraine

concentration.area: The Hauts-de-Meuse between Verdun and Toul, 19–26 August

sources.note: Added because this entity's only other source cannot be opened from here. p. 251: "In einer 'Ordre particulier Nr. 14' vom 19. August wurde die Bildung einer Armee de Lorraine unter General Maunoury angeordnet, die die Aufgaben der Gruppe Durand übernahm", with the 65th and 75th Reserve Divisions to be railed to Sorcy west of Toul between the 21st and the 23rd. p. 470 gives the divisions that were to join it where they stood on the evening of the 20th — the 73rd at Domèvre north of Toul, the 55th north of Thiaucourt, the 56th at Woël–Doncourt, the 72nd inside Verdun, the 54th on the heights between Ornes and Samogneux — under Durand, who was still commanding; p. 471 has Maunoury reach Verdun on the evening of the 21st and take over. So the army was ordered into being on the 19th and had its named commander on the 21st, which is why this record now begins on the 19th.

summary: A short-lived army of reserve divisions (the 3rd Group — 54th, 55th, 56th — with the 65th, 67th and 75th) under Maunoury to cover the gap between Verdun and Toul; ordered into being on 19 August, commanded by Maunoury from the evening of the 21st, broken up on 26 August, its commander and two divisions going west to form the 6th Army.

name: French VII Corps
summary: Besançon: 14th and 41st Divisions. Mulhouse on 8 August, then the Army of Alsace, then railed west to Maunoury's 6th Army for the Ourcq.

sources.note: Appendix 3, 'Order of Battle of the French Armies in August 1914': the VII. Corps (14th and 41st Divisions) under General Bonneau, in the First Army. The depot region and the corps' campaign are not from this appendix.

Corps (35th and 36th Divisions) under General Mas-Latrie, with the footnote that it was transferred to the Fifth Army and operated on the right flank of the BEF. name: French IV Corps

sources.note: Appendix 3, 'Order of Battle of the French Armies in August 1914': the IV. Corps (7th and 8th Divisions) under General Boelle, in the Third Army. The depot region and the corps' campaign are not from this appendix.

name: French 3rd Group of Reserve Divisions
summary: 54th, 55th and 56th Reserve Divisions; briefly the Army of Lorraine, two of them then railed to Paris for the 6th Army.

summary: Limoges: 23rd and 24th Divisions. Neufchâteau in the Ardennes; the Meuse; the Marne.

name: French II Corps

summary: 1st, 3rd and 5th Cavalry Divisions. Rode into the Ardennes on 6 August, covered the BEF's left at Mons and Le Cateau, then passed to the 6th Army at Paris; Bridoux replaced Sordet on 8 September.

sources.note: Appendix 3, 'Order of Battle of the French Armies in August 1914': the Cavalry Corps under General Sordet with the 1st (Buisson), 3rd (de Lastour) and 5th (Bridoux) Cavalry Divisions. The depot region and the corps' campaign are not from this appendix.

name: French Cavalry Corps (Conneau)
summary: 4th, 8th and 10th Cavalry Divisions, formed 31 August on the 5th Army's left; the Marne between the 5th Army and the BEF.

sources.note: The footnote to Appendix 3: 'Early in September three of the cavalry divisions (2nd, 8th and 10th) of the First and Second Armies were formed into a cavalry corps under General Conneau.' Edmonds gives the 2nd where this card gives the 4th, and 'early in September' rather than 31 August.

name: French Paris reserve divisions (61st, 62nd)
summary: The 61st and 62nd Reserve Divisions from the Paris garrison, given to Maunoury for the Ourcq.

sources.note: 'two French Reserve divisions, the 61st and 62nd (General Ebener's Group), had been sent from Paris to Arras' (p. 118); and on 5 September Ebener's Group stood behind Maunoury's Sixth Army (p. 282).

name: French Moroccan Brigade
summary: Ditte's Moroccan brigade, railed to the 6th Army; the Ourcq.

sources.note: The Moroccan Brigade counted in the Sixth Army's composition on 5 September.

name: British Expeditionary Force

sources.note: The war establishment of a division, some 18,000 all ranks (p. 6), and of the Cavalry Division, some 9,000 (p. 7); Appendix 2 prints the detail — 18,073 all ranks for a division (p. 487) and 9,269 for the Cavalry Division (p. 486). The volume does not print a single figure for the force on 21 August; 80,000 is a round total.

concentration.area: Maubeuge–Le Cateau, on the left of Lanrezac's 5th Army

sources.note: The concentration areas: 'a pear-shaped area between Maubeuge and Le Cateau, about twenty-five miles long from north-east to south-west, and averaging ten miles wide', with the cavalry at the north-eastern end 'ready to join hands with the French Fifth Army', and the corps areas listed one by one; the concentration 'was virtually complete on the 20th' (p. 50).

summary: I Corps (Haig) and II Corps (Smith-Dorrien), the Cavalry Division (Allenby) and the 19th Brigade — about 80,000 men on 21 August, near 100,000 once the 4th Division arrived on 25 August and III Corps was formed on 31 August. Mons, Le Cateau, the retreat to the Grand Morin, the advance into the gap, the Aisne.

sources.note: Appendix 1, 'Order of Battle of the British Expeditionary Force August 1914': GHQ, the Cavalry Division, the I., II. and III. Corps and their divisions, down to battalion and battery.

name: BEF I Corps
summary: 1st Division (Lomax) and 2nd Division (Monro) under Haig. In reserve at Mons; Landrecies on 25 August; the retreat, the Marne and the Aisne.

sources.note: Appendix 1: the I. Corps under Lieut.-General Sir D. Haig with the 1st Division (Major-General S. H. Lomax) and the 2nd Division (Major-General C. C. Monro).

name: BEF II Corps
summary: 3rd Division (Hamilton) and 5th Division (Fergusson). Grierson died on 17 August; Smith-Dorrien took over on the 21st. Mons on 23 August, Le Cateau on 26 August.

sources.note: Appendix 1: the II. Corps with the 3rd Division (Major-General Hubert I. W. Hamilton) and the 5th Division (Major-General Sir C. Fergusson), and the command note — Grierson '(Died in the train, between Rouen and Amiens, 17th August 1914)', Smith-Dorrien '(Took over command of II. Corps at Bavai, 4 p.m., 21st August 1914)'. The narrative (p. 50) gives Grierson's death as 'suddenly in the train on the morning of the 17th'.

name: BEF III Corps
summary: Formed 31 August under Pulteney from the 4th Division (Snow, landed 23 August, fought at Le Cateau) and the 19th Brigade; the 6th Division joined on the Aisne.

sources.note: Appendix 1: 'III. Corps (Formed in France, 31st August 1914)' under Major-General W. P. Pulteney, with the '4th Division (Landed in France, night 22nd/23rd August)' under Major-General T. D'O. Snow and the '6th Division (Embarked for St. Nazaire 8th/9th September 1914)'. The narrative (p. 50) has the 19th Brigade formed on 19 August under Major-General L. G. Drummond from four battalions taken off the lines of communication, which the appendix lists at p. 483.

name: BEF Cavalry Division
summary: Allenby: 1st–4th Cavalry Brigades, with the independent 5th Cavalry Brigade (Chetwode). Casteau on 22 August — the BEF's first shots — Mons, Le Cateau, the screen on the retreat.

sources.note: Appendix 1: the Cavalry Division under Major-General E. H. H. Allenby with the 1st to 4th Cavalry Brigades, and separately the '5th Cavalry Brigade (and attached troops)' under Brigadier-General Sir P. W. Chetwode; Appendix 2 (p. 486) gives its strength as 9,269 all ranks with 9,815 horses and twenty-four 13-pdrs.

name: Belgian Field Army

sources.note: 'Actually in August 1914 only 117,000 could be mobilized for the Field Army', and the six divisions listed on the same page.

concentration.area: On the Gette between Tienen (Tirlemont) and Diest, covering Brussels and Antwerp

sources.note: 'under cover of the 3rd Division, the 1st, 2nd, 5th and 6th Divisions were to move to the line of the river Gette, the Cavalry Division and detachments from Liège and Namur screening the movement… The concentration began on the 4th August' (p. 33); the German cavalry came before the Gette line on the 10th and attacked it at Haelen, south-east of Diest, on the 12th (p. 35).

summary: Six infantry divisions and a cavalry division, about 117,000 men, under the King with Selliers de Moranville as chief of staff. Haelen on 12 August, the retreat to Antwerp on 20 August, the sorties of 24–26 August and 9 September, the Yser in October.

sources.note: 'Actually in August 1914 only 117,000 could be mobilized for the Field Army' (p. 19), with the peacetime station of each division on the same page — 1st around Ghent, 2nd Antwerp, 3rd around Liège, 4th Namur and Charleroi, 5th around Mons, 6th Brussels, Cavalry Division Brussels; and Appendix 5 (p. 492) names their commanders and gives a division as between 25,500 and 32,000 all ranks and the Cavalry Division as 4,500.

summary: Ghent. The Gette, Antwerp, the Yser.

summary: Liège, under Leman: the defence of the interval between the forts on 5–6 August, then withdrawn to the field army on the Gette.

summary: Namur, under Michel: the defence of the fortress 20–24 August, then by way of France to Antwerp.

name: Belgian 5th Division
summary: Mons. The Gette, Antwerp.

sources.note: 'Actually in August 1914 only 117,000 could be mobilized for the Field Army' (p. 19), with the peacetime station of each division on the same page — 1st around Ghent, 2nd Antwerp, 3rd around Liège, 4th Namur and Charleroi, 5th around Mons, 6th Brussels, Cavalry Division Brussels; and Appendix 5 (p. 492) names their commanders and gives a division as between 25,500 and 32,000 all ranks and the Cavalry Division as 4,500.

name: Belgian 6th Division
summary: Brussels. The Gette, Antwerp.

sources.note: 'Actually in August 1914 only 117,000 could be mobilized for the Field Army' (p. 19), with the peacetime station of each division on the same page — 1st around Ghent, 2nd Antwerp, 3rd around Liège, 4th Namur and Charleroi, 5th around Mons, 6th Brussels, Cavalry Division Brussels; and Appendix 5 (p. 492) names their commanders and gives a division as between 25,500 and 32,000 all ranks and the Cavalry Division as 4,500.

name: Belgian Cavalry Division
summary: De Witte: Haelen on 12 August, where the German cavalry attacks broke on dismounted fire — the 'battle of the silver helmets'.

sources.note: Haelen, 12 August: 'six German cavalry regiments, with three horse-batteries and two Jäger battalions attacked the line of the Gette at Haelen… but were ultimately driven back by the Belgians, with appreciable loss, after ten hours of sharp fighting' (p. 35); Appendix 5 (p. 492) gives the division under Lieut.-General de Witte, two brigades, 4,500 all ranks and twelve guns.

name: Fortified position of Liège
summary: Twelve forts around Liège with the 3rd Division and fortress troops under Leman — about 30,000 men; resisted 4–16 August until the 42-cm and 30.5-cm howitzers broke the forts.

name: Fortified position of Namur
summary: Nine forts around Namur with the 4th Division and fortress troops under Michel; attacked from 20 August, the forts fell by 24–25 August to the same heavy howitzers.

name: Fortified position of Antwerp
summary: The national redoubt — an outer ring of forts twenty kilometres out and an inner ring — into which the field army withdrew on 20 August. Its garrison and the field army together tied down the III Reserve Corps, for a time the IX Reserve Corps, and then the Marine Division and Landwehr; besieged from 28 September and surrendered on 10 October.

sources.note: 'The Siege of Antwerp 28 Sept.' (p. 32), where the defences are described: 'an outer ring of 18 forts some seven to nine miles from the city, an inner line of older forts only two to three thousand yards from it, and a continuous enceinte' — seven to nine miles, not the twenty kilometres this card gives; the field army 'only 65,000 strong' and the garrison 'some 80,000 men' (p. 35); the field army's withdrawal on the night 6th/7th October, the eight forts of the inner line left to the fortress troops (p. 47); and the capitulation signed at Contich on the evening of 9 October, agreed and formally surrendered on the morning of the 10th (p. 62).

name: Fortified position of Maubeuge
summary: The French fortress on the Sambre — six forts and seven intermediate works built against the guns of 1880, about a thousand officers and 48,000 men of garrison and services, reservists and Territorials for the most part — invested by the VII Reserve Corps from 25 August and held until 7 September: longer than Liège or Namur, and long enough that the corps besieging it missed the Marne.

sources.note: 'Maubeuge was invested by the VII. Corps on the south-east and by the IX. Corps (of the First Army) on the north-west' — the volume names the VII. Corps, not Zwehl's VII. Reserve Corps, at the moment of investment, and prints no figure for the garrison.

name: 1st Army railhead
summary: Where the 1st Army's supply trains ended — the railhead creeping forward behind the demolitions from Aachen through Liège and Brussels, never closer than a hundred kilometres to the marching corps after the Sambre; beyond it, horse-drawn columns. Schematic positions (sand-1l0.21).

name: 2nd Army railhead
summary: Where the 2nd Army's supply trains ended — Liège, Namur and Charleroi by the end of August, with Maubeuge blocking the line south until 7 September. Schematic positions (sand-1l0.21).

name: French Tenth Army

concentration.area: Arras and the Scarpe, formed from corps railed north out of the Aisne and Lorraine

sources.note: The Tenth Army in line on the British right in the Race to the Sea, from Joffre's plan of 6 October. The volume does not print the army's concentration area at its formation.

summary: Improvised on 1 October 1914 as the Détachement d'armée de Maud'huy and regularised as the Tenth Army: the third French attempt to reach round the German northern flank, which instead found the German Sixth Army coming the other way and settled into the line before Arras.

sources.note: Joffre's plan of 6 October, under which 'the Second (General de Castelnau) and the Tenth (General Maud'huy) Armies, under direction of General Foch, were to continue the action they had begun against the right flank of the enemy in the "Race to the Sea"' (p. 69); and Maud'huy's own letter of 26 October to the G.O.C. II. Corps, signed as commanding the X Army (pp. 92–93). The volume's narrative begins on 19 September and does not print the army's formation on 1 October.

name: French Detachment in Belgium

concentration.area: Flanders, between the Belgians on the Yser and the British before Ypres; named, and d'Urbal in command, on 20 October

sources.note: p. 147, under 20 October: "On this day General d'Urbal took over command of the French forces in the north, which were now given the name of 'Le Detachement d'Armee de Belgique'; and he established his headquarters at Rousbrugge (7 miles north-west of Poperinghe)." That is the day this formation begins, and it is why the date here is the 20th and not the 15th: p. 103 shows what was in Flanders on 15 October — Bidon's 87th and 89th Territorial Divisions between Poperinghe and Ypres, the Naval Brigade at Dixmude — French troops in the north, but not yet this detachment. The Brigade de Fusiliers Marins under Rear-Admiral Ronarc'h, "6,000 seamen and 2,000 Zouaves" (p. 42), holds Dixmude in the line as given at p. 120.

summary: The French divisions, territorials and cavalry sent into Flanders in October 1914 under d'Urbal — including Ronarc'h's fusiliers marins at Dixmude. Regularised as the Eighth Army in November.

sources.note: 'On this day General d'Urbal took over command of the French forces in the north, which were now given the name of "Le Detachement d'Armee de Belgique"; and he established his headquarters at Rousbrugge' — the volume dates that to 20 October, not 15 October (p. 147). The Brigade de Fusiliers Marins under Rear-Admiral Ronarc'h, '6,000 seamen and 2,000 Zouaves' (p. 42), holds Dixmude in the line as given at p. 120.

name: German XXII Reserve Corps

concentration.area: Raised in Germany in August–September 1914; detrained west and south-west of Brussels, in full progress by 13 October, and marched into Flanders

sources.note: p. 122 is where this concentration point comes from: "The transport of the new corps of the Fourth Army to the Western Front began on the 10th October; by the 13th their detrainment was in full progress west and south-west of Brussels; and on the 14th they began their advance westwards in four columns to the line Eecloo (15 miles east of Bruges)—Deynze—Wortegem (4 miles west of Audenarde)", and "on the 17th the heads of the XXII., XXIII., XXVI. and XXVII. Reserve Corps reached a line about twenty miles from the Yser, defined by a point six miles east of Courtrai—Thielt—Oostcamp", standing on the evening of the 18th "in their appointed positions on a line Courtrai to Thourout". The volume gives the four corps one detrainment area and does not say which of them stood where inside it, so all four corps are placed at the same point on 13 October; only from the 17th do their paths follow each corps' own front.

summary: One of the four reserve corps raised after mobilization and thrown into Flanders in October 1914, half-trained, under the reconstituted Fourth Army.

sources.note: The new corps of the Fourth Army: the XXII. Reserve Corps, on the German right against the Belgians on the Yser, its left directed on Dixmude on 19 October (p. 168). The volume gives their raising on pp. 122–123 — Falkenhayn's reasons for engaging them in Flanders, and Balck's account of the formation of the 51st Reserve Division of the XXVI. Reserve Corps, in which '75 per cent of the new corps consisted of volunteers, untrained men over or under military age'.

name: German 8th Army
summary: The single army left to hold East Prussia while seven went west. Commanded by Prittwitz to 23 August, then by Hindenburg with Ludendorff as chief of staff. No route: this pack renders it as order of battle for the eastern cross-reference, not as a token on the western map.

name: Russian First Army
summary: Rennenkampf's army, which entered East Prussia from the east on 17 August and fought at Gumbinnen on the 20th. No route: order of battle for the eastern cross-reference only.

name: Russian Second Army
summary: Samsonov's army, which advanced north-west into East Prussia and was encircled at Tannenberg on 26-30 August. No route: order of battle for the eastern cross-reference only.
